question: What is @ControllerAdvice in Spring MVC?
title: @ControllerAdvice in Spring MVC — Global Exception Handling
direct_answer: @ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that makes an exception-handling class global — its @ExceptionHandler methods apply to all @Controller and @RestController classes in the application. It's the standard way to handle exceptions in a REST API with consistent error responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of centralized exception handling in production Spring Boot REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Handling exceptions in every controller method individually instead of using a global handler, leading to inconsistent error responses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate a complete @ControllerAdvice example with a structured error DTO, proper HTTP status codes, and mention that it supports @Order for multiple advice classes

sections.title: Global Exception Handler for REST APIs
sections.content:
**@ControllerAdvice** is a Spring annotation that creates a global exception handler for your entire REST API. Without it, you'd have to write @ExceptionHandler methods in every single controller, leading to code duplication and inconsistent error responses. When any @RestController throws an exception, Spring scans for a matching @ExceptionHandler method in your @ControllerAdvice class and routes the exception there.

Think of it as a **centralized error desk** in an office building — instead of every department handling complaints differently, one team handles all issues consistently with standardized responses. The class typically contains multiple @ExceptionHandler methods, each handling a different exception type (ResourceNotFoundException returns 404, ValidationException returns 400, etc.). This pattern is essential in production because clients expect consistent error structures regardless of what went wrong. @ControllerAdvice works seamlessly with @ResponseStatus and ResponseEntity to control HTTP status codes. It can also use @InitBinder for form validation and @ModelAttribute for shared model data, though exception handling is its primary purpose in REST APIs.

sections.title: @ControllerAdvice at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@ControllerAdvice|~Global exception handler|one class for all controllers|holds @ExceptionHandler methods|cross-cutting
blue|@RestControllerAdvice|~+ @ResponseBody|returns JSON error bodies|preferred for REST|same idea
emerald|How|~Exception propagates out|Spring routes to the advice|matching handler runs|clean separation
rose|Trap|~Per-controller handlers|duplicated logic|use global advice|DRY error handling

sections.title: Complete Global Exception Handler with Error DTO
When to Use @ControllerAdvice
sections.content: Use @ControllerAdvice in every Spring Boot REST API project from day one — it's not optional for production code. **Apply it when** you need consistent error responses across all endpoints, so clients can reliably parse errors regardless of which controller threw them. **Use it for** handling domain-specific exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException, InvalidInputException, or UnauthorizedException with appropriate HTTP status codes (404, 400, 401). **Essential for** validation failures where you need to return field-level error details in a structured format. In microservices, each service should have its own @ControllerAdvice to maintain consistent error contracts. If you have multiple advice classes (e.g., one for security, one for business logic), use @Order to control precedence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Handling exceptions inside controllers**: Freshers often write try-catch blocks in every controller method instead of letting exceptions bubble up to @ControllerAdvice, resulting in duplicated error-handling code and inconsistent responses.
- **Returning stack traces to clients**: Exposing ex.printStackTrace() or raw exception messages in production leaks internal implementation details and is a security risk — use generic messages for unexpected errors.
- **Forgetting HttpServletRequest parameter**: Not injecting HttpServletRequest in handler methods means you can't include the request path in error responses, making client-side debugging harder.
- **Not handling generic Exception**: If you only handle specific exceptions, unhandled ones will return Spring's default Whitelabel error page, breaking your API contract.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@ControllerAdvice**: annotates a global exception handler class that applies to all controllers in the application
**@ExceptionHandler methods**: inside @ControllerAdvice catch specific exception types thrown from any controller
**ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse>**: standard return type to control both HTTP status code and error body structure
**Consistent error DTOs**: use the same ErrorResponse record for all exception types so clients parse errors uniformly
**HttpServletRequest parameter**: inject to include request path and other context in error responses
**Catch-all handler**: always include an @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) method to handle unexpected errors gracefully
**@Order annotation**: use when multiple @ControllerAdvice classes exist to define precedence

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At-ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that creates a global exception handler for your entire REST API. It's critical because without it, you'd have to handle exceptions in every single controller, leading to inconsistent error responses. Here's how it works: when any controller throws an exception, Spring automatically routes it to a matching at-ExceptionHandler method inside your at-ControllerAdvice class. For example, if a service throws ResourceNotFoundException, your handler catches it and returns a structured error response with a 404 status code. The big advantage is consistency — all your endpoints return the same error structure, so clients can reliably parse errors. In production, you'd create an ErrorResponse record with fields like status, message, timestamp, and path. Then each handler method builds that DTO and wraps it in a ResponseEntity with the appropriate HTTP status. One mistake freshers make is handling exceptions inside controllers with try-catch blocks instead of letting them bubble up to the advice class. That duplicates code and breaks consistency. Another is returning raw exception messages to clients, which exposes internal details. Always include a catch-all handler for generic Exception to avoid Spring's default error page leaking through. In every Spring Boot project I'd work on, I'd set up at-ControllerAdvice on day one because it's not optional for professional REST APIs.

question: What is @ExceptionHandler in Spring MVC?
title: @ExceptionHandler in Spring MVC — Handling Specific Exceptions
direct_answer: @ExceptionHandler annotates a method that handles a specific exception type thrown from controllers. When that exception propagates out of a controller method, Spring calls the handler method instead of propagating the exception further, allowing you to return a custom response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the mechanics of exception handling in Spring MVC and how to map exceptions to HTTP responses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting @ExceptionHandler inside a @RestController thinking it's global — it only applies to that one controller
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly explain the difference between local (inside @RestController) and global (inside @ControllerAdvice) scope of @ExceptionHandler

sections.title: Exception Handler Method Annotation
sections.content:
**@ExceptionHandler** is a Spring annotation that marks a method as an exception handler. When a controller method throws an exception, Spring checks if there's an @ExceptionHandler method that can handle that exception type and calls it instead of letting the exception propagate to the servlet container.

The key is **scope**: if @ExceptionHandler is inside a @RestController, it only handles exceptions from that controller's methods. If it's inside a @ControllerAdvice class, it handles exceptions from **all controllers** in the application.

Think of it like **specialized customer service agents** — a local handler is like a department-specific agent who only handles issues from their department, while a global handler is like a centralized support team handling issues from anywhere. The handler method can accept the exception as a parameter, return a ResponseEntity to control the HTTP status code, and access HttpServletRequest for request details. This annotation is the foundation of Spring's exception handling mechanism. You specify which exception(s) to handle in the annotation value: @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class). Multiple exception types can be handled by one method using @ExceptionHandler({Ex1.class, Ex2.class}).

sections.title: @ExceptionHandler at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@ExceptionHandler|~Handles one exception type|method-level mapping|catches from controllers|returns a response
blue|Scope|~Local or global|in a controller = that one|in @ControllerAdvice = all|prefer global
emerald|Return|~ResponseEntity error|set status + body|map exception to HTTP code|user-friendly message
rose|Trap|~Catching broad Exception|catches everything|hides real errors|handle specific types first

sections.title: Local vs Global @ExceptionHandler
When to Use @ExceptionHandler
sections.content:
Use **local @ExceptionHandler** (inside @RestController) only when an exception is truly specific to one controller and shouldn't be handled globally — this is rare in practice. For example, a file upload controller might handle MultipartException locally with specific retry instructions.

Use **global @ExceptionHandler** (inside @ControllerAdvice) for all domain exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException, ValidationException, UnauthorizedException that can be thrown from any controller. **Always prefer global scope** to maintain consistent error responses across your API.

Use @ExceptionHandler for both checked and unchecked exceptions, though unchecked (RuntimeException subclasses) are more common in Spring. If you need to handle multiple related exceptions the same way, you can specify multiple exception classes in one handler method. Don't use @ExceptionHandler for business logic flow control — throw exceptions only for genuine error conditions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking local handlers are global**: Freshers often put @ExceptionHandler inside a @RestController expecting it to handle exceptions from all controllers — it only works for that one controller, leading to missed exceptions.
- **Not returning proper HTTP status codes**: Returning ResponseEntity.ok() from an exception handler defeats the purpose — clients need proper error status codes like 404, 400, or 500 to handle errors correctly.
- **Handling too broadly**: Writing @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) in a local controller catches all exceptions from that controller, hiding bugs that should propagate to global handlers.
- **Ignoring exception hierarchy**: If you have @ExceptionHandler for both RuntimeException and IllegalArgumentException, Spring chooses the most specific match, but freshers often don't realize the order matters when exceptions inherit from each other.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@ExceptionHandler**: annotates a method that handles specific exception types thrown from controllers
**Local scope**: when inside @RestController, it only handles exceptions from that controller's methods
**Global scope**: when inside @ControllerAdvice, it handles exceptions from all controllers in the application
**Exception parameter**: the handler method receives the thrown exception as a parameter to access its message and details
**ResponseEntity return**: return ResponseEntity to control both HTTP status code and response body structure
**Multiple exceptions**: can handle multiple exception types in one method: @ExceptionHandler({Ex1.class, Ex2.class})
**Most specific match**: Spring chooses the most specific handler when multiple handlers could handle an exception

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At-ExceptionHandler is an annotation that marks a method as an exception handler in Spring MVC. When a controller method throws an exception, Spring looks for an at-ExceptionHandler method that can handle that exception type and calls it instead of letting the error propagate. The critical thing to understand is scope. If you put at-ExceptionHandler inside a RestController, it only handles exceptions from that controller's methods — it's local. But if you put it inside a ControllerAdvice class, it handles exceptions from all controllers — it's global. In production, you almost always want global scope for consistent error handling. The handler method takes the exception as a parameter and returns a ResponseEntity so you can control the HTTP status code. For example, if a service throws ResourceNotFoundException, your handler catches it and returns a 404 response with a structured error body. One common mistake freshers make is putting exception handlers in controllers thinking they're global — then they wonder why exceptions from other controllers aren't caught. Another mistake is not returning proper status codes, just returning ok with an error message, which confuses clients. The best practice is to put all your at-ExceptionHandler methods in a single at-ControllerAdvice class so all exceptions are handled consistently across your API. That's how every production Spring Boot app I've seen does it.

question: How do you create a custom exception class in Spring Boot?
title: Custom Exception Classes in Spring Boot — ResourceNotFoundException Pattern
direct_answer: Create a class extending RuntimeException with a meaningful name like ResourceNotFoundException. Add a constructor that takes a message. Throw it from the service layer when a resource isn't found or business rules are violated. Catch it in @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler and map it to the appropriate HTTP status code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the full exception flow in a layered Spring Boot application from service to controller to client
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning null from service methods instead of throwing exceptions, forcing null checks everywhere and making the API contract unclear
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the complete flow: custom exception class → thrown in service → caught in @ControllerAdvice → structured HTTP response with correct status code

sections.title: Custom Exception Design Pattern
sections.content:
Creating custom exceptions is a fundamental pattern in Spring Boot applications for **expressing domain-specific errors** with clear intent. Instead of throwing generic IllegalArgumentException or returning null, you create exceptions like **ResourceNotFoundException**, **InvalidOrderException**, or **InsufficientBalanceException** that precisely describe what went wrong.

These exceptions extend **RuntimeException** (unchecked) so you don't force every caller to handle them with try-catch, keeping code clean. The pattern has three parts: (1) define the exception class with a constructor that takes a message, (2) throw it from the **service layer** when business rules are violated, and (3) catch it in **@ControllerAdvice** and map it to an HTTP status code like 404 or 400. Think of custom exceptions as **specific error codes** in an airport — instead of a generic "problem" announcement, you get "Flight AA123 delayed" which tells you exactly what's wrong. This approach makes errors **self-documenting** — when you see throw new OrderNotFoundException, you instantly know a resource lookup failed. Custom exceptions also enable consistent error responses because @ControllerAdvice handlers can return structured ErrorResponse DTOs tailored to each exception type. They're essential for clean separation of concerns — services throw domain exceptions, controllers never catch them, and @ControllerAdvice translates them to HTTP responses.

sections.title: Creating a Custom Exception
sections.content:
amber|Extend RuntimeException|~Unchecked exception|class ResourceNotFoundException|meaningful name|message constructor
blue|Throw it|~From the service layer|when a resource is missing|or a rule is violated|clear intent
emerald|Map to a status|~@ResponseStatus(NOT_FOUND)|or @ExceptionHandler|404 to the client|consistent codes
rose|Trap|~Checked exceptions|force try/catch everywhere|prefer RuntimeException|cleaner service code

sections.title: Complete Custom Exception Flow
When to Create Custom Exceptions
sections.content:
Create custom exceptions for **domain-specific error conditions** that need different HTTP status codes or error messages.

Use **ResourceNotFoundException** (404) when an entity lookup by ID fails — this is the most common custom exception in REST APIs. Create **ValidationException** (400) for business rule violations like "Order total cannot be negative" that aren't caught by bean validation.

Use **UnauthorizedException** (401) or **ForbiddenException** (403) for security violations. **Don't create custom exceptions** for programming errors like NullPointerException or IllegalStateException — let those propagate as 500 errors. Don't overdo it — if you have 20 custom exceptions that all return 400 with slightly different messages, you probably only need one ValidationException with different message parameters. Create a custom exception when you need **specific handling logic** in @ControllerAdvice, like logging to a separate audit table for payment failures. Extend RuntimeException for domain exceptions to avoid polluting method signatures with checked exception declarations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Returning null instead of throwing**: Freshers often return null from service methods when a resource isn't found, forcing every caller to check for null and leading to NullPointerExceptions in controllers — throw ResourceNotFoundException instead to fail fast with a clear error.
- **Extending Exception instead of RuntimeException**: Creating checked exceptions forces try-catch blocks everywhere, cluttering code and violating Spring's fail-fast philosophy for domain errors.
- **Throwing exceptions from controllers**: Controllers should never throw domain exceptions directly — they should call services which throw them, maintaining clean separation of concerns.
- **Creating too many exception types**: Having 15 different not-found exceptions (UserNotFoundException, OrderNotFoundException, etc.) creates maintenance overhead — use one ResourceNotFoundException with a descriptive message parameter instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **RuntimeException parent**: extend RuntimeException for domain exceptions to avoid checked exception boilerplate
**Meaningful names**: use names like ResourceNotFoundException or InvalidOrderException that clearly express what went wrong
**Service layer throws**: throw custom exceptions from the service layer, not controllers, to maintain separation of concerns
**Message parameter**: provide a constructor that takes a String message to give context about what failed
**@ControllerAdvice catches**: handle custom exceptions in @ControllerAdvice to map them to HTTP status codes and structured errors
**Fail fast principle**: throw exceptions immediately when business rules are violated instead of returning null or error flags
**One exception per HTTP status**: consider using one ResourceNotFoundException for all 404 cases instead of 10 different not-found exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To create a custom exception in Spring Boot, you extend RuntimeException and give it a meaningful name that describes the error. For example, ResourceNotFoundException for when an entity isn't found. You add a constructor that takes a String message so you can provide context. Then you throw this exception from your service layer methods. For instance, in OrderService when you look up an order by ID and it doesn't exist, you throw new ResourceNotFoundException with a message like "Order not found with id: 42". The key is you don't catch this exception in the controller. Instead, you let it bubble up to a ControllerAdvice class where you have an at-ExceptionHandler method that catches ResourceNotFoundException and converts it to a proper HTTP response — usually a 404 status with a structured error body. This pattern keeps your code clean because services express domain errors clearly, controllers don't have try-catch blocks everywhere, and all error responses are consistent. A common mistake freshers make is returning null from service methods when something isn't found. That forces null checks everywhere and makes it unclear to clients what happened. Another mistake is extending Exception instead of RuntimeException, which makes it a checked exception and forces try-catch blocks all over the place. In production, you'd have a few core custom exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException for 404s, ValidationException for 400s, and maybe UnauthorizedException for 401s. You don't need 20 different exception types — keep it simple and use descriptive messages to differentiate cases.

question: What is a good error response structure for a REST API?
title: REST API Error Response Structure — Best Practices
direct_answer: A good REST error response includes: HTTP status code (in body for convenience), user-friendly error message (not stack traces), timestamp, request path, and optionally field-level errors for validation failures. Use a consistent DTO structure across all error types so clients can parse errors reliably.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of API design principles and client-server contracts for error communication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning different error structures for different exceptions, making it impossible for clients to parse errors consistently
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete ErrorResponse DTO with all essential fields and mention RFC 7807 Problem Details standard for HTTP APIs

sections.title: Standardized Error Response Structure
sections.content:
A well-designed REST API error response is a **contract between server and client** that enables reliable error handling. The structure must be **consistent** — every error, whether it's a 404 not-found or a 400 validation failure, should return the same JSON shape so clients can parse it once and handle all errors uniformly. Core fields include: **status code** (like 404 or 400, duplicated in the body for convenience even though it's in HTTP headers), **message** (human-readable explanation of what went wrong), **timestamp** (when the error occurred, useful for debugging and correlating with server logs), and **path** (the request URI that caused the error, so clients know which endpoint failed). For validation errors, add a **fields** map or array with field-name-to-error-message mappings.

Think of it like a **standardized medical report** — regardless of what test you took, the report format is consistent with date, patient info, test name, and results in predictable locations. **Never return stack traces** to clients in production — they expose internal implementation details and are security risks. Use generic messages for unexpected errors ("An internal error occurred") while logging full details server-side. Modern best practice is **RFC 7807 Problem Details**, a standard format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields. Spring Boot 3 has built-in support for this via ProblemDetail class.

sections.title: A Good Error Response
sections.content:
amber|Good error body|~Consistent shape|status + message|timestamp + path|machine + human readable
blue|Field errors|~For validation|list of field + reason|helps the client fix input|from @Valid failures
emerald|Hide internals|~No stack traces|no SQL or class names|safe, clean message|log details server-side
rose|Trap|~Leaking stack traces|security risk|inconsistent formats|standardize one structure

sections.title: Complete Error Response DTOs with Validation Support
When to Use This Structure
sections.content:
Use a standardized error response DTO in **every REST API** you build — it's not optional for production systems.

Apply it from day one when you create your first @ControllerAdvice class. **Use ErrorResponse** (simple DTO with status, message, timestamp, path) for all single-error cases: resource not found, unauthorized access, business rule violations. **Use ValidationErrorResponse** (adds fieldErrors map) specifically for bean validation failures from @Valid annotations where multiple fields can have errors simultaneously. **Include timestamp** always — it's critical for correlating client errors with server logs when debugging production issues. **Include path** always — clients often make parallel requests to different endpoints and need to know which call failed. For microservices, consider adding a **traceId** field that propagates through distributed logs. If you're building a public API, document your error response structure in OpenAPI/Swagger specs so consumers can code against it reliably. For very simple internal APIs, you might skip timestamp, but status, message, and path are non-negotiable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inconsistent error structures**: Freshers often return {"error": "message"} for one exception type and {"message": "error", "code": 404} for another — clients can't parse this reliably, breaking error handling.
- **Exposing stack traces**: Returning ex.getStackTrace() or ex.toString() in production leaks internal class names, file paths, and logic flow — use generic messages for unexpected errors and log details server-side only.
- **Missing HTTP status in body**: Relying solely on HTTP headers for status codes forces clients to check both headers and body structure differently — include status in the body for convenience.
- **Not including request path**: When clients make multiple parallel API calls and one fails, they can't tell which endpoint caused the error without the path field.
- **Using different DTOs per exception**: Creating ResourceNotFoundError, ValidationError, AuthError with different field names makes client parsing complex — use one DTO shape with optional fields.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Consistent structure**: use the same JSON shape for all error responses so clients parse errors uniformly
**status field**: include HTTP status code in the body for convenience even though it's in headers
**message field**: human-readable explanation of what went wrong, user-friendly, not technical stack traces
**timestamp field**: when the error occurred, essential for correlating with server logs during debugging
**path field**: the request URI that caused the error, critical when clients make parallel requests
**fieldErrors for validation**: add a map of field names to error messages for bean validation failures
**RFC 7807 Problem Details**: modern standard format supported by Spring Boot 3 via ProblemDetail class

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A good REST error response needs to be consistent and informative. The most important thing is using the same JSON structure for all errors so clients can parse them reliably. You need four core fields. First, the HTTP status code like 404 or 400 — include it in the body even though it's in the headers for convenience. Second, a user-friendly message that explains what went wrong, like "Order not found with id 42". Never return stack traces or technical details to clients. Third, a timestamp showing when the error occurred — this is critical for debugging because you can correlate it with server logs. Fourth, the request path, like "/api/orders/42", so clients know which endpoint failed, especially when making multiple parallel requests. For validation errors, you'd extend this structure with a field-errors map, where each key is a field name and the value is the error message, like "email": "must be a valid email address". The pattern is to create an ErrorResponse record with these fields, then in your ControllerAdvice exception handlers, build this DTO and wrap it in a ResponseEntity with the appropriate status code. A common mistake freshers make is returning different error structures for different exceptions — maybe one returns just a string message and another returns a complex object — that breaks client error handling. Another mistake is exposing stack traces in production, which is a security risk. If you want to follow modern standards, there's RFC 7807 Problem Details for HTTP APIs, which Spring Boot 3 supports natively through the ProblemDetail class. It defines fields like type, title, status, detail, and instance. But even if you don't use that standard, the key is consistency — pick a structure and use it everywhere.

question: What is ResponseEntityExceptionHandler in Spring MVC?
title: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler — Base Class for Spring MVC Exception Handling
direct_answer: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is a Spring base class that provides centralized exception handling for common Spring MVC exceptions. When your @ControllerAdvice extends it, you automatically get proper HTTP status codes and error responses for exceptions like MethodArgumentNotValidException (400), NoHandlerFoundException (404), and HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException (405).

sections.title: Built-in Exception Handler Base Class
sections.content:
**ResponseEntityExceptionHandler** is a convenience base class provided by Spring MVC that handles most standard Spring framework exceptions automatically. When you extend this class in your **@ControllerAdvice** or **@RestControllerAdvice**, you inherit pre-configured exception handlers for about 20 common Spring MVC exceptions — things that happen during request processing, validation, method argument binding, and HTTP method mismatches. Each handler maps the exception to the appropriate **HTTP status code** (400, 404, 405, 415, etc.) and returns a **ResponseEntity** with a default error body. This saves you from writing boilerplate exception handlers for framework-level errors. The class is designed to be extended — you override specific **protected methods** (like `handleMethodArgumentNotValid()`) when you want to customize the error response while keeping the correct status code.

Think of it as Spring's **safety net** — it catches common mistakes (invalid JSON, wrong HTTP method, missing path variables) and gives clients meaningful HTTP responses instead of generic 500 errors.

sections.title: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler
sections.content:
amber|ResponseEntityExceptionHandler|~Base class for advice|handles Spring MVC exceptions|extend in @ControllerAdvice|consistent defaults
blue|Built-in handling|~Validation, 404, 415|MethodArgumentNotValid etc.|proper status codes|override to customize
emerald|Override|~handleMethodArgumentNotValid|shape the error body|call super or replace|add your format
rose|Trap|~Reinventing handlers|duplicates Spring's work|extend the base class|override only what differs

sections.title: Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler for Custom Validation Errors
When to Use ResponseEntityExceptionHandler
sections.content: Use **ResponseEntityExceptionHandler** when building a REST API that needs consistent error handling across all endpoints. Extend it in your **@RestControllerAdvice** class whenever you want to customize how Spring's built-in exceptions are returned to clients — for example, changing the validation error format from Spring's default structure to your own **ErrorDTO** shape. It's especially useful when you need to add custom fields like **timestamp**, **requestId**, or **errorCode** to all error responses while keeping Spring's correct HTTP status codes. Don't use it if you're only handling custom business exceptions (like **OrderNotFoundException**) — in that case, a plain **@RestControllerAdvice** with **@ExceptionHandler** methods is simpler. Also skip it if you want complete control over every exception and don't need Spring's default mappings.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Handling Spring exceptions twice**: Freshers often write an `@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)` method in their advice class that already extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler — this creates a conflict because the base class already handles it. The correct approach is to **override** the protected `handleMethodArgumentNotValid()` method instead.
- **Not calling super when needed**: When overriding a handle method, freshers sometimes write completely custom logic and forget that calling `super.handleXxx()` can provide a good starting point. If you just want to add logging, call super and wrap the result.
- **Wrong exception names**: Confusing `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (validation failures on **@Valid** DTOs) with `ConstraintViolationException` (validation failures on method parameters with **@Validated** on the class). ResponseEntityExceptionHandler only handles the first one by default.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Base class purpose**: Provides pre-configured handlers for ~20 standard Spring MVC exceptions with correct HTTP status codes
**Extension mechanism**: Extend it in your @RestControllerAdvice and override protected handleXxx() methods to customize responses
**Status code preservation**: Keeps Spring's correct status codes (400, 404, 405) while letting you change the response body structure
**Common exceptions handled**: MethodArgumentNotValidException, NoHandlerFoundException, HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException, TypeMismatchException, HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException
**Override pattern**: Override handleMethodArgumentNotValid() to customize validation error format — don't write a separate @ExceptionHandler for it
**When not needed**: If you only handle custom business exceptions or want full control over all exception responses, a plain @RestControllerAdvice is simpler
**Spring Boot default**: Even without extending it, Spring Boot has basic error handling — extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler gives you fine-grained control over each exception type

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is a base class from Spring MVC that you extend in your RestControllerAdvice to get automatic handling of common Spring exceptions. When your advice class extends it, you inherit handlers for about twenty standard exceptions — things like MethodArgumentNotValidException when validation fails, NoHandlerFoundException when a route doesn't exist, or HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException when someone sends a POST to a GET endpoint. Each of these gets mapped to the right HTTP status code automatically. The cool part is you can override specific methods to customize the response. For example, if you override handleMethodArgumentNotValid, you can change how validation errors are formatted — maybe you want a list of field errors in a specific JSON structure — but you still get the 400 Bad Request status code that Spring provides. One mistake freshers make is writing a separate ExceptionHandler method for MethodArgumentNotValidException when their advice already extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. That creates a conflict because the base class already handles it. You should override the protected method instead. Use this when you're building a REST API and want consistent error responses across all endpoints while keeping Spring's correct HTTP status behavior. It saves you from writing boilerplate for framework-level exceptions so you can focus on handling your own business exceptions.

question: What are best practices for exception handling in a Spring REST API?
title: Exception Handling Best Practices in Spring REST API
direct_answer: Best practices for Spring REST exception handling include: use @RestControllerAdvice for centralized global handling, create specific custom exceptions for different business errors (ResourceNotFoundException, InvalidOrderException), return consistent error response DTOs with fields like message, timestamp, and status, map exceptions to appropriate HTTP status codes (404 for not found, 400 for validation, 409 for conflicts, 500 for server errors), and always log exceptions server-side with context for debugging while never exposing stack traces to clients.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of production-ready error handling architecture and awareness of security, consistency, and debugging concerns in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Catching all exceptions with a single Exception handler returning 500, or worse, sending stack traces to clients in production
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the five pillars — global advice, meaningful exceptions, consistent DTOs, correct status codes, server-side logging — and explain why each matters for client experience and debugging

sections.title: Production-Ready Exception Strategy
sections.content:
Exception handling in a REST API isn't just about catching errors — it's about creating a **consistent contract** between your backend and clients (web, mobile, third-party integrations) so they can handle errors predictably. Best practices revolve around five pillars: **centralized handling** with **@RestControllerAdvice** (one place for all error logic), **meaningful custom exceptions** that represent specific business failures (not generic RuntimeException), **consistent error DTOs** that always have the same JSON shape, **correct HTTP status codes** that match REST semantics (404 for missing resources, 400 for bad input, 409 for conflicts), and **server-side logging** of full exception details while returning **safe sanitized messages** to clients. The goal is **developer experience** for API consumers (they can parse errors programmatically), **security** (no stack traces or internal paths exposed), and **debuggability** (logs have enough context to fix issues).

Think of it like a **well-designed error API** — predictable, informative, never leaking internals.

sections.title: Exception Handling Best Practices
sections.content:
amber|Global handling|~@RestControllerAdvice|one place for all errors|consistent responses|no scattered try/catch
blue|Specific exceptions|~Per business error|ResourceNotFound, Conflict|map each to a status|clear semantics
emerald|Standard body|~status + message|timestamp + path|field errors for validation|documented contract
rose|Trap|~Catch and swallow|or expose stack traces|log + return a clean error|never leak internals

sections.title: Complete Exception Handling Setup with Best Practices
When to Apply Each Best Practice
sections.content: Use **@RestControllerAdvice** from day one of your REST API — it prevents scattered try-catch blocks in controllers and ensures all exceptions are handled consistently. Create **custom exceptions** whenever you have a distinct business failure mode: ResourceNotFoundException for missing entities, InvalidOrderStatusException for state transition errors, DuplicateEmailException for uniqueness violations. Map each to the **appropriate status code**: 404 for not found, 400 for client input errors, 409 for conflicts, 422 for unprocessable entities, 500 for server bugs. Always return a **consistent ErrorResponse DTO** with the same fields (message, status, timestamp, path, optional details array) so mobile and web clients can parse errors the same way across all endpoints. Log the **full exception with stack trace** using SLF4J or Log4j2 at ERROR level for 500s and WARN level for 404s and 400s — but return a **sanitized message** to clients that doesn't reveal internal class names, database column names, or file paths.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Catching Exception.class only**: Freshers often write a single ExceptionHandler for `Exception.class` that returns 500 for everything. This lumps not-found errors, validation failures, and server bugs into one bucket — clients can't differentiate between "you sent bad data" (400) and "our server crashed" (500). The fix is to handle specific exceptions with correct status codes first, then have a catch-all Exception handler as a last resort.
- **Returning stack traces to clients**: Another common mistake is including `ex.printStackTrace()` output or exception class names in the JSON response. This leaks internal implementation details (package names, database types, library versions) that attackers can exploit. Always log the full trace server-side and return a generic message to clients.
- **Inconsistent error formats**: Returning `{"error":"message"}` from one endpoint, `{"message":"...","code":123}` from another, and plain strings from a third. Clients can't reliably parse errors. Define one ErrorResponse record and use it everywhere.
- **Not logging exceptions**: Freshers sometimes return an error response but forget to log the exception. When a production bug happens, there's no trace in the logs to debug.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Centralized handling**: Use @RestControllerAdvice to handle all exceptions in one place instead of try-catch in every controller method
**Meaningful exceptions**: Create custom exception classes per business failure (ResourceNotFoundException, InvalidOrderException) with context fields like resourceId
**Consistent error DTO**: Define one ErrorResponse record with message, status, timestamp, path, details — use it for all error responses across all endpoints
**Correct HTTP status codes**: 404 for not found, 400 for validation/bad input, 409 for conflicts, 422 for unprocessable entities, 500 for server errors — never return 200 with an error payload
**Server-side logging**: Log full exception with stack trace at ERROR or WARN level — include request context (user ID, endpoint, parameters) for debugging
**Never expose internals**: Return sanitized messages to clients — no stack traces, class names, SQL errors, or file paths in JSON responses
**Exception hierarchy**: Handle specific exceptions first (ResourceNotFoundException), then broader categories (RuntimeException), then catch-all (Exception) last

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The best practices for exception handling in a Spring REST API come down to five key areas. First, use RestControllerAdvice to centralize all your exception handling in one global class instead of scattering try-catch blocks across controllers. This keeps your error logic consistent and your controllers clean. Second, create meaningful custom exceptions for different business failures — like ResourceNotFoundException when an order doesn't exist or InvalidOrderStatusException when someone tries an illegal state transition. This lets you handle each case with the right HTTP status code and error message. Third, always return a consistent error response structure. Define an ErrorResponse record with fields like message, status, timestamp, and path, and use it everywhere. Clients — whether they're your web frontend, mobile app, or third-party integrations — can then parse errors reliably. Fourth, map exceptions to the correct HTTP status codes. Use 404 for not found, 400 for bad input or validation failures, 409 for conflicts like duplicate emails, and 500 only for actual server errors. This follows REST conventions and helps clients decide whether to retry or show a user message. Fifth, always log the full exception with stack trace server-side at ERROR or WARN level, but never send that detail to clients. Return a safe, sanitized message instead. One common mistake freshers make is having a single Exception handler that returns 500 for everything. That makes it impossible for clients to distinguish between different error types. Another is including stack traces in the JSON response, which leaks internal implementation details. Following these five practices gives you production-ready error handling that's secure, debuggable, and provides a great developer experience for anyone consuming your API.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: There are five pillars to solid exception handling in a Spring REST API.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Centralize: use @RestControllerAdvice as the single place for all error responses.
Meaningful exceptions: name them after what went wrong — ResourceNotFoundException, DuplicateEmailException — not generic RuntimeException.
Consistent error DTO: same JSON structure for every error type so clients parse reliably.
Correct HTTP codes: 400 for bad input, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts, 500 for unexpected errors.
Log server-side: use log.error with the exception — the stack trace goes to your logs, never to the client.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The layering principle matters too: the service layer throws domain exceptions that mean something business-wise. The @ControllerAdvice translates them to HTTP. The service never knows about HTTP status codes and the controller never knows about business rules.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: Testing error paths is just as important as testing success paths. A @ControllerAdvice that works for the 404 case but breaks for the 409 case is a production bug waiting to happen. Write MockMvc tests for each exception handler.

speakable_v2.cap: If your service layer knows about HTTP status codes, something is wrong. If your controller has business logic in catch blocks, something is wrong.
